title: Zen centers in the West
hookLine: Zen centers founded by Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese teachers

lines: A TEACHER WHO CROSSED AN OCEAN.
cards: A row of shoes by a door on a city street: sneakers, work boots, a pair of heels, lined up neatly on a wooden rack. Upstairs, in a room that used to be an office, people in dark clothes sit facing a white wall.
A wooden board is struck outside, then a bell inside. No one moves. Not long ago some of them were on the subway.
Rooms like this exist in cities and farmhouses across Europe and the Americas, and this one, like others, traces back to a teacher who crossed an ocean.

teach.b: Day nine forty-eight followed Zen west in D. T. Suzuki's books; today, the teachers who built its halls.
First, the name. Tradition traces the word Zen back through the Chinese Chan to the Sanskrit dhyana, meditation.
So the name had already traveled, from India to China, and from China to Korea, Japan and Vietnam, where it's called Seon and Thien. Second, the teachers.
Western Zen centers were founded by teachers from more than one of those homes. From Japan came teachers such as Shunryu Suzuki, who helped found the San Francisco Zen Center.
From Korea came Seung Sahn, whose students formed the Kwan Um School. From Vietnam came Thich Nhat Hanh, met at the start of this week.
Each brought the chants, forms and flavor of his own country, so a Japanese-style zendo and a Korean-style dharma room don't feel quite the same. Third, what they faced.
These teachers arrived far from home, teaching students who knew little of Buddhist culture. Some Western students wanted meditation without the bowing and chanting.

teach.h: WHAT TO KEEP, WHAT TO TRANSLATE.
teach.b: The teachers had to decide what to keep, what to translate and what to let go, and they didn't all decide the same way.

teach.h: A WEEK OF PRACTICE ON THE MOVE.
teach.b: Fourth, the week. It started with engaged Buddhism and the stretcher, then went to hospices and prisons, to Taiwan's temples, schools and relief teams, to the family altar, and to people living together.
Zen in the West closes it the way it began: practice carried a long way from where it started, and still recognizably itself.

how: Western Zen centers hold daily or weekly sitting periods, often facing a wall or the center of the room, with chanting, bowing and talks in the style of the Japanese, Korean or Vietnamese lineage that founded them.

games.q: what does “zen centers in the west” mean?
o: meditation halls in the West founded by teachers from Asia
Western retreats that teach calm without any Buddhist roots
Japanese temples that send their monks to train in Europe

from Korea, the Kwan Um School
Zen's names in Korea and Vietnam

teachers came from Japan, Korea and Vietnam, each with their own forms.
tradition traces the word Zen back to the Sanskrit dhyana
the teachers all agreed on what to keep for Western students
they had to choose what to keep, translate or let go, and they chose differently.

games.q: you're a Zen teacher newly arrived in an American city. your students want meditation but find the bowing and chanting strange. what do you do?
o: keep every form exactly as at home.
decide, piece by piece, what to keep and what to translate.
games.why: teachers faced exactly this choice, and they didn't all decide the same way. that's one reason Western Zen centers differ from each other.

practice: Sit upright, hands resting in your lap, eyes lowered, facing a plain wall if there's one near you. Let the breath be ordinary, and count each out-breath, one to ten, starting again whenever you lose count.
That's all: some version of what teachers from Japan, Korea and Vietnam taught, far from home, to people who had never sat before.

wordCard.voice: Zen centers in the West. Meditation halls in Europe and the Americas founded by teachers from Japan, Korea and Vietnam, each carrying the forms of home. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhyana: meditation. Tradition traces Chinese Chan, Korean Seon, Vietnamese Thien and Japanese Zen back to it.

carryVoice: Your line: far from home. A row of shoes, and a wall to face. Back tomorrow, same hill.
